heading: 11.13 Aggregation and concentration of risk, credit failure
text:
11.13 Aggregation and concentration of risk, credit failure — Aggregation of risk:
The combined effect of all the individual risks of loss must be considered, allowing for the correlations and interactions between them. Model office projections will be used to assess the overall risk, typically using stochastic modelling and sensitivity testing.

file: 5. Risks/11.13 Aggregation and concentration of risk, credit failure.md
heading: 11.13 Aggregation and concentration of risk, credit failure
text:
11.13 Aggregation and concentration of risk, credit failure — Concentration of risk:
Concentration risk arises when a life insurer has a high variance in claim costs due to a small number of very large exposures or risks that are not independent. Which could be as a result of:
- Large individual exposures e.g. a very high sum assured
- Non-independent risks e.g. policyholders are exposed to the same event/accident/disaster
- Geographic or occupation clustering e.g. concentration of policyholders in a specific region or occupation

Concentration risk can also manifest on the asset side of the balance sheet:
- Asset over-concentration e.g. being overly dependent on the success of a single asset class or the shares of an individual company.
- Counterparty credit failure e.g. relying on a single reinsurer

file: 5. Risks/11.13 Aggregation and concentration of risk, credit failure.md
heading: 11.13 Aggregation and concentration of risk, credit failure
text:
11.13 Aggregation and concentration of risk, credit failure — Credit failure:
An insurance company's credit rating is an external assessment of the aggregation of all the risks it is exposed to, performed by credit rating agencies. The insurer will arrange its business practices and overall risk profile such that it minimises the possibility of being downgraded (or leads to the credit rating being upgraded).
A downgrading of a company's credit rating is a risk because it would lead to:
- Reputational damage
- Greater difficulty and cost of raising additional capital in the market

and as a consequence:
- The range of profitable activities may be constrained
- Increased lapses and reduced new business.

heading: 11.14 Actions of distributors
text:
11.14 Actions of distributors — Risks from distributors:
Distributors, such as insurance intermediaries and brokers, can introduce financial and operational risks through several behaviors:

• Lapse and Re-entry: Distributors may encourage policyholders to cancel existing policies and take out new ones if there are no exit penalties or commission "clawbacks". This results in a loss for the insurer if the profit from the new policy fails to cover the loss of future profits from the original contract and the new acquisition costs.

• Exploitation of Product Design: Intermediaries may take advantage of loopholes in risk classification, such as finding ways to get a policyholder accepted at non-smoker rates despite their actual health status.

• Unit Pricing Arbitrage: In unit-linked business, distributors might exploit timing differences in unit pricing by cashing in units after a market fall but before the insurer has updated the daily price.

• Credit Risk (Broker Balances): Insurers are exposed to the risk that brokers collect premiums from policyholders but delay or fail to pass those funds to the company.

• Mis-selling and Legal Risk: If a distributor makes representations to a client that are inconsistent with the policy document, the insurer faces potential legal action, regulatory intervention, and reputational damage.

heading: 11.15 Operational risk
callout_header: Failure of management systems and controls
text:
11.15 Operational risk — Failure of management systems and controls:
Risk arises from the possibility that directors fail to impose or adequately monitor systems of control. Even if systems are documented, they may be contravened due to insufficient monitoring, leading to financial losses, regulatory intervention, and reputational damage. For instance, a failure to implement a pricing control system correctly might result in the company selling loss-making products

heading: 11.15 Operational risk
text:
11.15 Operational risk — Fraud:
- Directors or staff: Because directors have special access to financial and banking systems, as well as the computer programs and data supporting the business, they are in a position to perpetrate deliberate fraud. This type of control failure caused by deliberate intent can lead to immediate and severe losses for the insurer.
- Policyholders: the main risk here relates to fraudulent claims, the risk increasing in proportion to the difficulty of detection. Countries with secure processes for certifying deaths represent reduced risks.
- Other outside parties: such parties may effectively obtain some access to the computer systems of the insurer, particularly where there are external components such as website access.

heading: 11.16 Risk and decision-making
text:
11.16 Risk and decision-making — Risk and decision-making:
Risk of loss has to be measured in terms of the effect it may have on the aims of the company. These aims are:
- to maximise profits, and/or
- to maximise the return on capital

Risk must also be assessed in relation to:
- the company's capital and other resources
- its impact on supervisory solvency
- the cost of failing to meet any other legislative requirements

The insurance company will make its strategic decisions by balancing the trade of between risk and return, which could be expressed as"
- finding the appropriate risk-return combination, or
- maximising expected return subject to an acceptable degree of risk.

heading: 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk
text:
11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Components of mortality/morbidity risk:
There are three risks associated with mortality/ASSA/F102 Life Insurance Principles/Definitions/morbidity assumptions:
- Model risk: the assumed probability distribution could be inappropriate e.g assuming policyholders are i.i.d, with  $Bin(n, p)$. The failure of these assumptions about the population i.e. independent, identical and the type of distribution with respect to mortality would increase the risk.
- Parameter risk: the specific model parameter estimates e.g. $p$  used in the model may not reflect actual population parameters even though the underlying model is appropriate.
- Random fluctuations: unpredictable variations due to sample size (too low for the law of large numbers to apply).

The likelihood of our assumptions for the future being correct depends on the quality, credibility and relevance of the data available.

heading: 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk
callout_header: Influences on model and parameter uncertainty
text:
11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Influences on model and parameter uncertainty:
Insurers must constantly update their assumptions, but several factors make this process risky:
- Medical advances
- Data inadequacy
- Expanding funnel of doubt
- Capital and reserving impact

heading: 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk
text:
11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Directions of mortality risk:
The impact of mortality depends on the nature of the insurance contract:
- Mortality: For life insurance products like term assurance, the risk is that deaths are higher than expected, leading to a reduction in profit or capital shortfall. The risk is most significant at the start of a contract when the sum at risk is at its highest.
- Longevity: For survival-contingent products like immediate annuities, the risk is that policyholders live longer than expected. In this scenario, the insurer risks paying out more income than they had initially priced for through the initial single premium and reserved for.

See mortality question example: Question 13.3

heading: 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk
text:
11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Selection risks:
Mortality experience is heavily influenced by the behaviour and health status of policyholders:
- Anti-selection
- Selective withdrawals

heading: 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk
callout_header: Claims experience for health and care products
text:
11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Claims experience for health and care products:
Claims experience for IP, CI and LTCI is significantly more difficult to manage and model because benefits are contingent on health states rather than death.
- The primary risk for health and care contracts is due to the scarcity of reliable, credible and relevant data due to  data issues for health and care contracts.
- The primary risk for IP involves transfer probabilities in a multi-state model: the rate at which healthy lives fall sick (inception) and the rate at which sick lives recover or die (termination)
- For CI, the main risk is the rate of diagnosis for the specific illnesses listed in the contract.
- The main risk for LTCI relates to claim inception rates and the probabilities of moving between different states of care,. e.g., from home care to nursing home care.

heading: 11.3 Investment risk
text:
11.3 Investment risk — Components of investment risk:
- Model risk: there is a danger that the chosen mathematical model for future investment returns (e.g. the probability distribution for equity returns) is an inappropriate representation of reality.
- Parameter risk: even with an appropriate model, there is the risk that the specific values used to parameterise the model (such as the mean return, variance or correlations between asset classes) might be incorrectly estimated.
- Random fluctuations: future investment performance may not correspond exactly with the model or parameters adopted, even if those inputs are judged to be appropriate.

heading: 11.3 Investment risk
text:
11.3 Investment risk — Mismatching risk:
This involves a discrepancy between the discounted mean term (duration) of the assets and the liabilities
- Reinvestment risk: If assets have a shorter duration than liabilities, proceeds are available earlier than required and must be reinvested at unknown future rates. If interest rates fall, the insurer may be unable to secure the yields needed to meet long-term guarantees
- Capital values risk: If assets have a longer duration than liabilities, the insurer may be forced to sell assets to meet claims. If interest rates rise, the market value of the assets will fall more than the value of the liabilities, potentially causing insolvency.

heading: 11.4 Expense risk
text:
11.4 Expense risk — Components of expense inflation risk:
When assumptions are made about future expenses to be incurred by the company, these will allow for inflation (either on a deterministic or stochastic basis) . There is therefore a parameter risk. In addition there will be a model risk if stochastic assumptions are being used. Inflation assumptions are also subject to an Expanding funnel of doubt and random fluctuations.

heading: 11.4 Expense risk
callout_header: The link between inflation and investment returns
text:
11.4 Expense risk — The link between inflation and investment returns:
The differential between the return on government fixed-interest securities and index-linked securities is a specific link used to estimate inflation expectations. Model risk is high if inflation and investment returns are not dynamically linked within the model.

heading: 11.4 Expense risk
text:
11.4 Expense risk — Sources of expense risk:
Expense risk stems from the possibility that future reality will differ from the assumptions made when the products were originally priced. The risk that the charges/loadings received are lower than expected is typically classified as other types of risk depending on the driver of the shortfall:
1. New business mix or volume risk: fixed overheads must be spread over fewer policies, the actual per-policy cost will rise above the level assumed in pricing. Conversely. inappropriately high volumes can overstretch administrative resources leading to inefficiencies and mistakes
2. Inflation risk: if inflation is higher than expected, the fixed expense loadings built into premiums (especially on level premiums) may become insufficient to cover actual escalating costs.
3. Withdrawal (Persistency) risk: if a policy withdraws early, the insurer may fail to receive enough premiums to recover initial expenses
4. Investment risk: in unit linked contracts where charges are a percentage of the fund value, a drop in investment returns reduces the value of those charges, creating a shortfall for meeting fixed expenses.

heading: 11.5 Withdrawal risk
text:
11.5 Withdrawal risk — Components of withdrawal risk:
The estimation of future withdrawals which encompasses surrenders, lapses and making policies paid up is a fundamental source of risk for insurers, primarily because policyholder behaviour often deviates from actuarial assumptions. The risks in the estimations include:
- Model risk: arises when an inappropriate framework to predict behaviour is used. such as incorrectly assuming that withdrawal rates are linked to specific variables like investment returns or GDP.
- Parameter risk: even if the model is correct, there is a risk that the parameters used (the specific rates) are wrongly estimated, such as generally underestimating the level of future withdrawals.
- Random fluctuations: in smaller insurance portfolios, the actual number of withdrawals can vary unpredictable due to sample error, even if the underlying parameters and model are correct.

heading: 11.5 Withdrawal risk
callout_header: Withdrawals as a driver of mortality risk
text:
11.5 Withdrawal risk — Withdrawals as a driver of mortality risk:
In actuarial investigations, risks are dynamically linked, withdrawals are treated as a driver variable for mortality. In a multiple decrement model, mortality and withdrawal are dependent rates due to the effect of selective withdrawals. If the withdrawal parameter is wrongly estimated, the mortality rate becomes fundamentally incorrect.

heading: 11.5 Withdrawal risk
callout_header: Withdrawals as a driver of expense risk
text:
11.5 Withdrawal risk — Withdrawals as a driver of expense risk:
A similar relationship exists between withdrawal rates and expense parameters.
1. Spreading of fixed costs
- Expense assumptions for in-force business are calibrated based on a model of future new business and withdrawals
- If actual withdrawals are higher than the modelled parameter (the withdrawal rate), the company's fixed overhead costs must be spread over fewer policies.
- This invalidates the previous expense parameter, as the actual per-policy expense becomes higher than what was allowed for in the pricing or reserving basis.

The relationship between withdrawals and expenses is a direct dynamic mathematical link driven by the allocation of fixed costs.

2. Recouping initial expenses
- The pricing model calculates charges/premiums based on a specific assumed withdrawal rate to ensure the company receives enough income over time to cover the initial capital strain.
- When actual withdrawal behaviour departs from the estimate and policyholders leave earlier than expected,
- The future charges required to repay the initial acquisition costs are never received - the company incurs an immediate loss.

While the is a financial shortfall is in the company's ability to cover its expenses, it is specifically classified as Withdrawal (Persistency) risk.

heading: 11.5 Withdrawal risk
callout_header: Withdrawals as a driver of investment risk
text:
11.5 Withdrawal risk — Withdrawals as a driver of investment risk:
Withdrawal estimation directly influences the discounted mean term of liabilities which can lead to mismatching risk.

heading: 11.5 Withdrawal risk
callout_header: What is the impact of changes in lapse assumptions on the reserves?
text:
11.5 Withdrawal risk — What is the impact of changes in lapse assumptions on the reserves?:
Lapses have opposing effects on different elements of the reserve.
- Future premiums
- Future benefits
- Future expenses
- Negative reserves
- The overall effect is uncertain

file: 5. Risks/11.6 Mix of new business risk.md
heading: 11.6 Mix of new business risk
text:
11.6 Mix of new business risk — Mix by Nature:
The "nature" of a contract refers to its fundamental structure and classification. Changes in this mix include shifts between:
- Class of between: e.g. the proportion of pensions business written
- Type of contract: e.g. term assurances vs endowments
- Contract design: e.g. with-profits vs unit linked
- Premium frequency: single vs regular premium

When the capital required to write these different products or the inherent risks (such as investment or mortality risk) vary across these categories, the company's overall capital needs and risk exposure will change along with the fluctuations.

file: 5. Risks/11.6 Mix of new business risk.md
heading: 11.6 Mix of new business risk
text:
11.6 Mix of new business risk — Mix by size:
The risk related to contract size primary concerns expense recovery. Many insurance expenses are fixed per policy, meaning they are incurred at the same level regardless of the policy's sum assured or premium size. Conversely, the income from charges and premium loadings is often a proportion of the premium.
- Average size reduction: If new contracts are smaller on average than assumed in pricing, the total income from charges will be reduced, but expenses will not decrease by the same margin, leading to a mismatch the company may fail to cover its fixed costs.
- Cross-subsidies: Companies often accept a degree of cross-subsidy where larger contracts subsidize the fixed costs of smaller ones. An unintended shift toward smaller policies erodes this subsidy potentially making the product line loss making.

file: 5. Risks/11.6 Mix of new business risk.md
heading: 11.6 Mix of new business risk
text:
11.6 Mix of new business risk — Mix by Source (distribution channel):
The distribution channel used to sell the policy, is a source of risk because:
- Demographics: different channels reach different populations, with varying mortality, morbidity and withdrawal experience.
- Distribution costs: salespeople's remuneration and commission levels vary by channel

An insurer may wish to charge the same price for a product through all its distribution channels despite the different expected experience (due to the above). It would therefore set mortality and expense assumptions based on a weighted average of the expected mix of business by source. If the actual mix differs from the expected source, these parameters may be invalidated, leading to less profit than anticipated or even suffer a loss. To mitigate the risk arising for the mix by source, the company can price its products differently for each distribution channel (dual pricing), as each channel remains independently profitable.

heading: 11.7 Volume of business risk
text:
11.7 Volume of business risk — Too high volumes:
- Initial capital strain will use up the company's free assets (the excess of assets over liabilities), potentially leading to a situation where capital resources become inadequate to support further growth or continued solvency.
- Rapid growth can over-stretch the company's administrative resources, leading to inefficiencies, processing delays or underwriting mistakes. These failure can damage the company's reputation and create secondary marketing risks.

heading: 11.7 Volume of business risk
text:
11.7 Volume of business risk — Too low volumes:
- Failure to cover fixed overheads: if volumes are lower than expected, the actual average expense per policy will rise, eroding profit margins.
- Recovering development costs: If sales are too low, the company risks never recovering the up-front costs of developing and marketing the product line.
- Long-term viability: a significant fall in business volumes will damage the company's competitiveness and eventually threaten its long term viability as it becomes less able to achieve economies of scale.

heading: 11.8 Guarantees and options risks
text:
11.8 Guarantees and options risks — Mortality and morbidity guarantees:
The main risks are:
- Anti-selection by poor health individuals
- Initial Capital strain from higher capital requirements
- Parameter and model risk

heading: 11.8 Guarantees and options risks
text:
11.8 Guarantees and options risks — Investment guarantees:
The primary risk is that assets will be insufficient to cover the guarantee:
- Investment mismatch risk
- Financial selection on American style options (guaranteed surrender values)

heading: 11.8 Guarantees and options risks
text:
11.8 Guarantees and options risks — Parameter and model risk:
To offer a guarantee or option, actuaries must estimate its future cost:
- Model risk: The framework used to calculate the cost may be an over-simplification of reality. For example using a deterministic model to value an investment guarantee might suggest a zero cost of the best estimate/mean return is high, whereas a stochastic model would reveal a positive cost by accounting for the variability of investment returns.
- Parameter risk: even if the model is appropriate, the specific values used to calibrate the model (such as future interest rates or mortality improvements) may be incorrectly estimated.

heading: 11.8 Guarantees and options risks
callout_header: Managing the risks associated with options & guarantees
text:
11.8 Guarantees and options risks — Managing the risks associated with options & guarantees:
Companies manage the risks of options and guarantees through product design, financial hedging and rigorous valuation.

heading: 11.9 Competition risk
text:
11.9 Competition risk — Impact on Pricing and Profitability**:
Competitive pressure often leads insurers to reduce premium rates or charges for new business contracts to match or undercut rivals. In highly price-sensitive channels, such as independent intermediaries, companies might set charges that cover only the marginal costs of a policy, thereby failing to make an adequate contribution to the company's fixed overhead expenses. If the total contribution from all products falls below the level of these fixed overheads, the company’s overall profitability is directly threatened. Furthermore, competition may prevent an insurer from increasing reviewable charges on existing business even when the underlying claims or expense experience has worsened.

heading: 11.9 Competition risk
text:
11.9 Competition risk — Onerous Guarantees and Options:
To differentiate their products in a crowded market, companies may offer additional guarantees and options at little or no extra cost to the policyholder. Historically, competition has pushed some insurers into offering guarantees before the true cost of reserving for those future risks was fully estimated or priced. These features increase risk because the company commits to specific terms—such as guaranteed annuity rates or minimum maturity values—decades before the actual cost is known.

heading: 11.9 Competition risk
text:
11.9 Competition risk — Bonus and Distribution Pressures**:
In the with-profits market, insurers may feel compelled to increase bonus declarations beyond what the underlying asset shares can sustainably support to maintain a competitive position against other offices. Similarly, competition for "shelf space" within distribution channels can lead to higher commissions for intermediaries or increased salaries for sales forces. These higher acquisition costs increase the initial capital strain on the company, meaning more capital is required to write each new policy.

heading: 11.9 Competition risk
text:
11.9 Competition risk — Compounding Effect of Business Volume**:
The risks associated with competitive pricing and generous guarantees are often compounded by high volumes of new business. While high sales are typically a goal, writing an unexpectedly large volume of capital-intensive business can deplete an insurer’s free assets and required solvency margins. If the company has reduced its margins to be competitive, it may find that it lacks the capital resources to support its own rapid growth, potentially leading to supervisory insolvency.

heading: 11.9 Competition risk
text:
11.9 Competition risk — Marketing and Reputational Risks**:
Failure to remain competitive can lead to a bad reputation in the market, which travels fast and damages future sales. However, if an insurer over-promises through competitive bonus rates and then must cut them to reflect "financial reality," it faces marketing risk and potential policyholder dissatisfaction. This disappointment can lead to increased withdrawals (lapses), which further increases the actual average administrative cost for the remaining policies

12 Unit pricing and actuarial funding — Unit pricing:
This whole chapter is concerned with one aspect of a unit-linked product.
- A unit-linked benefit is determined by the performance of units. This performance is determined by the performance of the underlying assets.
- Pricing a unit is assessing the value of assets attributable to one unit in the fund.

heading: 12 Unit pricing and actuarial funding
text:
12 Unit pricing and actuarial funding — Principal risks in unit pricing:
- Timing risk: Unit prices are set at discrete points in time, while asset values move continuously
- Asset values are volatile
- Sudden movements in asset values
- Outdated asset valuations (property)
- Approximations
- tax on unrealised gains
- accrued interest
- Errors: Incorrect data/calculation errors
- Wrong basis (appropriation vs expropriation price)
- Regulatory changes (restrictions on charges included in the unit price)
- Reputational risk: from violating basic equity principle or unclear communication
- Anti-selection: Policyholder selection against the company if the price overstates the asset value

The words bid and offer are used in three different situations:
- to refer to the buying and selling prices of assets
- to refer to the buying and selling prices of units

12 Unit pricing and actuarial funding — Actuarial funding:
Is the idea that, for unit-linked policies that have level (ongoing) charges to cover initial expenses, we can reduce the first year's capital strain by holding an adjusted reserve, by taking into account the expected income from charges to reduce the initial capital strain:

file: 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding/12.1 Unit pricing.md
heading: 12.1 Unit pricing
text:
12.1 Unit pricing — Appropriation and expropriation prices:
To maintain this equity, insurers distinguish between the price at which units are created and the price at which they are cancelled.
- Appropriation price: this is the price at which the company creates a unit. It is calculated on an offer basis, i.e. using the market's "offer price" for the underlying assets plus purchases expenses, taxes and accrued income.
- This represents the amount of money of money that must be put into the fund for the creation of a unit
- Expropriation price: this is the price at which the company cancels a unit. It is calculated on a bid basis, i.e. using the market's "bid price" (the proceeds from selling the assets minus sale expenses)

file: 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding/12.1 Unit pricing.md
heading: 12.1 Unit pricing
text:
12.1 Unit pricing — Unit pricing:
1. The appropriation price is the price at which a unit would be created determined as:
- the net asset value of the fund on an offer basis
- divided by the number of existing units at the time of the calculation
2. The net asset value of the fund on an offer basis is calculated as:
1. The market value of the assets obtained from the exchange (mark-to-market)
2.  If some assets do not have an observable market value, e.g. property a professional valuation may be needed
3. Alternatively, a mark-to-model approach may be used. A model may project expected cashflows using financial economic assumptions  and the cashflows are discounted.
4. Any expenses involved in purchasing additional assets must be added (incl. stamp duty)
5. Current assets must be added (e.g. cash on deposit)
6. Current liabilities must be deducted (e.g. investments purchased but not yet settled)
7. Accrued income must be added (e.g. interest income on deposits) net of any outgo (e.g. charges)
8. Accrued tax must be deducted

file: 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding/12.1 Unit pricing.md
heading: 12.1 Unit pricing
text:
12.1 Unit pricing — Fund pricing bases:
The company must decide which pricing bases to use depending on the net cashflow of the fund.
- Offer basis: for an expanding fund where the insurer is a net creator of units
- Bid basis: for a contracting fund where the insurer is a net canceller of units

In practice, companies do not switch the basis daily based on minor fluctuations, instead, they use a broad equity approach where the basis only changes if there is a significant cashflow movement against the current basis.

12.1 Unit pricing — Pricing for policyholder:
Within either the offer or bid basis, the insurer quotes two prices to the policyholder.
- Offer price: the price at which the policyholder buys units from the company
- Bid price: the price at which the company buys units back from the policyholder.

The difference between these two is the bid-offer spread, which serves as an initial charge to meet management expenses, commissions and profit. The final quoted prices are often rounded up, which can be done in favour of either the company or the customer depending on company practice and regulation.

12.1 Unit pricing — Management box:
Some insurers maintain a management box, which is an excess of units owned by the company. This allows the company to manage day-to-day unit transactions without constantly buying or selling the underlying assets, which helps to minimize volatility. However the management box exposes the company to investment risk.

heading: 12.2 Actuarial funding
text:
12.2 Actuarial funding — definition:
Actuarial funding is a technique used by life insurance companies to capitalise charges above those needed for recurring expenses at inception. It reduces the total reserves held by the company thus reducing new business strain.
It eliminates investment risk because of the mismatch between initial expenses (generally a monetary amount) and charges (% of fund over time).

file: 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding/12.2 Actuarial funding.md
heading: 12.2 Actuarial funding
text:
12.2 Actuarial funding — Purpose and rationale:
Unit-linked contracts often incur very high initial expenses (such as commission and medical underwriting) that exceed the first premium, resulting in a large initial capital strain.

The practice of funding initial expenses through lower allocation rates during the early policy years is no longer common and lower premium allocation rates are not consistent with PRE.

The expenses are usually recouped gradually via future fund management charges, this creates a mismatch in timing and nature between the immediate cash outgo and the gradual investment-linked income.

Actuarial funding addresses this by allowing the company to hold a smaller unit reserve at inception than the actual value of the units purchased by the premium. The company essentially "takes credit" in advance for a portion of the future management charges to cover its up-front costs.

file: 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding/12.2 Actuarial funding.md
heading: 12.2 Actuarial funding
text:
12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:
Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.
- Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be
$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$
- Where:
- $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
- $x$ is the entry age
- $n$ is the policy term
- Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.

file: 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding/12.2 Actuarial funding.md
heading: 12.2 Actuarial funding
text:
12.2 Actuarial funding — Conditions for use:
For actuarial funding to be viable and prudent, the following conditions must be met:
- High management charges: There must be a substantial level of regular management charges to "buy back" the missing units over the policy term.
- Higher management charges can be charged on all units, provided there is a sizeable quantity of FMC's to make the pre-funding worthwhile.
- In the early years allocated premiums would be used to buy capital units which have higher charges and accumulation units. - this practice is no longer popular due to transparency issues.
- Surrender penalties: It is not prudent to hold a reserve lower than what would be paid if the policyholder surrendered. Therefore, the funded reserve must not be less than the surrender value (bid value minus surrender penalty)
- Positive Future Cashflows: Projections must show that future net cashflows to the insurer remain positive even after the management charges are reduced to rebuild the reserve.
- Contingency: The benefit must be payable in a contingent event e.g. death or sickness

file: 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding/12.2 Actuarial funding.md
heading: 12.2 Actuarial funding
text:
12.2 Actuarial funding — Absence of investment risk:
The expected return on the unit fund is irrelevant to the discount rate because there is no investment risk in the buy-back process.
- The liability ($l$) (the missing units) is denoted in units: $l = (n-x)* UnitPrice$
- The source of funding (management charge) is a fixed percentage of the units. $FMC=percentagexUnitPrice$
- Therefore: $l \approx FMC$

If the unit fund doubles in value due to high investment returns, the monetary cost of buying the missing units also doubles. However, because the management charge is a percentage of that fund, the amount of money to buy those units also doubles. Because both the cost of the units and the funding source (the management charges) move in direct proportion to the unit price. The insurer effectively "borrows" units rather than cash, and since the "repayments" are also unit-linked, the investment risk is eliminated from the buy-back process

heading: 12.2 Actuarial funding
text:
12.2 Actuarial funding — example:
The setup:
- Single premium: R10 000 (purchasing 10 000 units at R1 each)
- Annual FMC: 5 (levied only on units physically held)
- Discount rate for funding $(i)$: 4%
- Policy term: 5 years
- Age ($x$): 40 year old
- Investment return $(g)$: 7%
- Actuarial funding factor ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$): A multiplier that determines the required reserve based on the 4% and the probability of the contingent events (death or maturity)
----
Year 0: Inception
At the start, the insurer calculates the actuarially funded unit reserve instead of holding the full R10 000.
- Funding factor ($A_{40:\overline{5|}}$): $0.8219$ (based on 4% discount over 5 years)
- Reserve physically held: $$V_0 = R 10,000 * 0.8219 = R 8,219$$
- Cashflow to non-unit fund: $R10,000 - R8,219$
- This positive cashflow is used to pay for initial expenses like commission and underwriting.
- The insurer is now missing $1,781$ units that it must buy back later.
---

heading: 13. Models
text:
13. Models — Chapter 13 — Models overview:
This chapter covers actuarial models used in life insurance, including:

- The purpose and types of actuarial models (deterministic, stochastic, scenario-based)
- Model design: inputs, assumptions, structure, and outputs
- Validation and verification of models
- Limitations of models and sources of model error
- The role of models in pricing, reserving, capital assessment and business planning
- Allowing for risk and uncertainty in model outputs

heading: 13.1 Objectives and requirements
callout_header: What are the known objectives for building a model?
text:
13.1 Objectives and requirements — What are the known objectives for building a model?:
Actuarial models provide the actuary with a tool to give appropriate advice to ensure the company is run on a sound financial basis. Models can be used for:
1. Financial projections
2. Budgeting and financial planning
3. Calculating provisions for claims
4. Proving solvency to the regulator
5. Pricing new/existing products
6. Setting actuarial assumptions
7. Calculating capital requirements
8. Business strategy
9. Valuing guarantees/options
10. Assessing reinsurance requirements

heading: 13.1 Objectives and requirements
callout_header: What are the requirements of a good model?
text:
13.1 Objectives and requirements — What are the requirements of a good model?:
Model requirements are VARIABLE CRISP DATA

- Valid (accuracy, passes fitness tests)
Adequately documented
Rigorous (mathematically sound)

heading: 13.2 Model components
text:
13.2 Model components — Model components:
To satisfy these requirements, the components of the model must allow for all those features of the business being modelled that could significantly affect the advice being given:
- Model points: These are data records representing homogeneous groups of policies chosen to reflect the distribution of the business without needing to model every individual policy.
- Parameters: A parameter must be included in the model if the decision reached would alter for different values of that parameter e.g. interest rates.
- Time period (frequency) of cashflow projection must be short enough to produce reliable results while being cost-effective.
- Future Cashflows: inclusion of all material cashflows, including premiums, investment income, benefit payments, expenses that are relevant to the business being modelled.
- Dynamic correlations: The ability to model interactions between assets and liabilities, such as bonus declarations moving in line with investment performance.
- Reserving cashflows: Allowance for the notional cashflows arising from setting up supervisory reserves and required solvency margins. The investment income from the supervisory reserve should also be included as a positive contribution to the profit flow.
- Stochastic capability: For products with financial guarantees or options, the model may need to use stochastic simulation (Monte Carlo methods) rather than deterministic approaches.

heading: 13.2 Model components
text:
13.2 Model components — Profit calculation:
The total profit arising over the year is the change in free assets and can be calculated as: $$Profit= (A_{t+1} - V_{t+1}) - (A_t - V_t) = (A_{t+1​}−A_t​)−(V_{t+1​}−V_t​)$$
Where:
- $(A_{t+1}​−A_t​)$ represents the change in total assets, which includes all physical investment income earned on the assets backing the reserves.
- $(V_{t+1}​−V_t​)$ represents the notional increase in the reserve liability.

heading: 13.2 Model components
callout_header: Distinction between real and notional cashflows
text:
13.2 Model components — Distinction between real and notional cashflows:
A supervisory reserve is a liability figure on a balance sheet, but it represents the amount physical assets that a company is legally required to set aside to meet future obligations.
- The increase in reserves is labelled "notional" because no money physically leaves the company, it is simply moved on the balance sheet from a category of free assets to required assets.
- Real contribution: because these assets are physically held by the company, they earn real investment income
The investment income on the reserve ($V$) is a "real" positive contribution because it increases the total pool of assets ($A$) available to the company

heading: 13.3 Stochastic versus deterministic
text:
13.3 Stochastic versus deterministic — Stochastic vs deterministic:
A stochastic approach may be preferred, because:
- we need to find the cost of guarantees and options
- we would wish to see the likely distribution of outcomes, not just a single estimate
- the interaction between variables can be explicitly included, enabling the effect of the interactions to be assessed
- we need to estimate a probability.

Deterministic modelling can be used:
- with sensitivity testing, in order to get an approximation to a stochastic result
- where the result obtained would be very similar to (or, if not, more prudent than) a stochastically produced result
- as a check on a stochastic model.

Stochastic models suffer from high sensitivity to the chosen parameter values, with the risk of ../../Definitions/Spurious accuracy. So we should only use stochastic modelling when the variable can be reliably modelled by a well-defined probability distribution.

heading: 13.4 Market-consistent approach
text:
13.4 Market-consistent approach — Traditional (passive) approach:
This method assumes a risk-free rate of return (such as on government bonds) and then adds a margin for the riskier assets like equities.

Assets may be valued using historic cost or book value, which is insensitive to short-term market changes.

Assumptions are typically derived from historical experience and industry data, often with added prudential margins to ensure solvency

heading: 13.4 Market-consistent approach
text:
13.4 Market-consistent approach — The financial economic (market-consistent) approach:
The financial economic approach assumes market-consistent values for parameters.

The assumed investment return should be the risk-free rate (regardless of asset type) as the potential additional returns from more risky assets should be exactly cancelled out by their increased risk.

Assets are valued at market value.
Market-consistent values of the liabilities can be calculated as the current market values of the (risk-free) assets that match the liability cashflows.

Assessing the market value of other (non-financial) aspects of the liability (like mortality) is more problematic. There may be some actual market valuations of liabilities available – e.g. for traded endowments.

heading: 13.5 Model uses
text:
13.5 Model uses — Pricing:
The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.
1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix
2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects
- withdrawal death and maturity benefits
- premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
- reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
- Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)
3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:
- mortality withdrawal and expenses
4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)
5. Time period: Month/annual
6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve
7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).
8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.
- NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
- IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
- DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.
9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.
10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..
11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

heading: 13.5 Model uses
text:
13.5 Model uses — Profitability of existing business:
12. Data: The assessment can be performed using:
- Full policy data: on a policy-by-policy basis, requires computing resources and time.
- Model points: group policies into homogeneous groups. Verification may be done by calculating the reserves on them and comparing them with the published value.
13. Cashflow projection: the model projects all real and notional cashflows for each policy or model point.
14. Discounting: the net cashflows are discounted back to the valuation date to determine the PVFP (Present Value of Future Profits which feeds into Embedded Value).
15. Risk discount rate (RDR): the RDR used for existing business is typically lower than the rate used for pricing new business because the risks associated with new business (e.g. uncertainty over sales volumes and mix of business) are no longer applicable to in-force policies.
16. Use of results: Management uses these models to gain insights such as:
- Breakdowns: analysing by product line, product class, distribution channel or subsidiary to compare relative contributions to the firm
- Financial health check: simply checking that the PVFP for a specific product is positive serves as an indicator that its nothing is badly going wrong with the financial management of that product.
- Appraisal value: when the company is valued for sale, the embedded value serves as the starting point, which is then added to goodwill (the value of future new business) to determine the appraisal value.

heading: 13.5 Model uses
text:
13.5 Model uses — Assessing solvency:
This assessment involves comparing the value of the company's assets against its liabilities using either supervisory (regulatory) or economic capital requirements.
17. Static vs dynamic: static solvency testing only measures a company's financial position at a single point in time, dynamic solvency testing uses a full model office to project the revenue account and balance sheet forward for 3 to 5 years.
- Assesses the company's resilience to changes in the external economic environment.
- Identify is the company's surplus assets might be likely to run out or become negative in the near future.
- Provide management with enough time to adjust strategies - such as changing investment strategy, reduce bonus distributions, or alter marketing plans - to reduce the risk of insolvency/
18. Deterministic vs stochastic: actuaries use deterministic projections to test the impact on solvency, of specific scenarios, such as a gradual fall in investment returns or faster-than-expected mortality improvements on. Regulators may specify which deterministic scenarios must be tested. Stochastic projections uses Monte Carlo simulations to generate thousands of potential future paths for variables like in the balance sheet and revenue account. This allows the actuary to quantify the probability of ruin.
19. Modelling challenges: When projecting solvency stochastically, a major computational challenge is nested simulations, where the projected balance sheet for a future year itself requires thousands of simulations to value complex features like financial guarantees or options. Closed-form approximations (such as the Black-Scholes formula) or proxy models can be used to estimate these values efficiently.
20. Probability of absolute ruin: for a closed fund (no new business), an actuary may project just the revenue account until the very last contract expires. If the accumulated net cashflow up to that time is positive, company is solvent for that run. The proportion of simulations where the company runs out of assets is the estimated probability of absolute ruin.
21. Solvency capital requirements (risk margin): Models are used to determine the level of required solvency capital, which acts as a protective cushion. Under risk-based regimes like Value-at-Risk (VaR), models subject the balance sheet to extreme "shocks" (such as a 1-in-200-year event) to ensure the company remains solvency over a defined period, usually over one year. This requires the model to account for the benefits of diversification within its portfolio as it is unlikely that all extreme risks will happen at the same time.

heading: 13.6 Sensitivity testing
text:
13.6 Sensitivity testing — Sensitivity testing:
Sensitivity tests show the vulnerability of the results to changes in assumptions (or unexpected future events).

Outcomes are analysed for sensitivity to variations in:
- model point assumptions (volumes & business mix)
- parameter values

Sensitivity testing, on a deterministic basis, can be used to determine the margins that may be necessary in a basis.

Such margins in each parameter can be a way of allowing for risk in a pricing model as an alternative to risk margins in the discount rate.

Sensitivity analysis can help to determine the variance of profit, or of the return on capital, where stochastic approaches are not viable.

heading: 13.7 Allowing for risk
text:
13.7 Allowing for risk — Risk discount rate:
The most common way to allow for the statistical risk associated with parameter values (assumptions) in cashflow modelling is by using a risk discount rate that includes a risk premium over the risk-free rate of return.


- Prudential margins in assumptions: such as using higher-expected mortality rates for life insurance products or lower than expected interest rates for savings products
- Stochastic modelling: assigning probability distributions to unknown parameters rather than a single value.
- the main difficulty is what probability distribution to assign and how to parameterize it, sensitivity analysis is a more pragmatic and transparent way to handle parameter risk without the risk of spurious accuracy caused by deciding upon some arbitrary probability distribution.

heading: 13.7 Allowing for risk
text:
13.7 Allowing for risk — Sensitivity analysis:
- Deterministic sensitivity analysis: involves varying one or more parameter values at a time to observe the financial impact on profit or solvency.
- Identifying Vulnerabilities: It helps the actuary understand which factors the product’s profitability is most sensitive to (e.g., if a 10% increase in lapses wipes out all profit).
- Scenario Testing: Actuaries can also test "scenarios" where several correlated variables are adjusted together, such as a high-inflation scenario combined with high interest rates

heading: 13.7 Allowing for risk
text:
13.7 Allowing for risk — Market consistent approach:
Liabilities are valued to be consistent with current market prices of assets that would replicate the liabilities cashflows, this approaches uses a combination of risk-free discount rates and the addition of explicit risk margins.
- risk-free discounting: future cashflows are discounted at the risk free rate
- risk neutral asset valuation: the expected investment returns are set to the risk-free rate regardless of the actual assets held, because any potential higher yield from risky assets is viewed as being offset by the increased risk of not achieving that yield.
- risk margins: because some risks (like mortality) are not traded, a risk margin is added to the best estimate.

heading: 14.10 Consistency with other products
text:
14.10 Consistency with other products — Consistency:
Maintaining consistency with the existing product range is essential for both operational efficiency and policyholder equity.
- Operational Efficiency: Similar charging and benefit structures across a product line save time and costs related to systems development, training administrative and sales staff, and printing marketing materials.

- Policyholder Equity: A design that appears significantly more attractive than existing business may be perceived as unfair by current policyholders. This dissatisfaction can lead to a marketing risk, where existing clients surrender their policies in mass, preventing the company from recovering its fixed overhead costs.

- Ease of Transition: Consistency ensures that new products align with the company's established brand and the expectations of its distribution channels.

file: 8. Product design/14.10 Consistency with other products.md
heading: 14.10 Consistency with other products
text:
14.10 Consistency with other products — Interaction of product design factors:
Product design factors are not independent; meeting one objective frequently prejudices another, meaning the final design must be an optimal compromise between customer needs and insurer objectives.
A core interaction exists between profitability and risk control versus marketability and competitiveness
Risk Management vs. Sales Volume: While rigorous underwriting and claims management reduce the risk of adverse experience, onerous processes can act as a barrier to sales, negatively impacting business volumes
Simplicity vs. Equity (Cross-subsidies): A simple charging structure is easier for customers to understand and for systems to handle, but it often creates conscious cross-subsidies where larger policies overpay to support the administration of smaller policies
Consistency vs. Innovation: New designs must be consistent with the existing product range to ensure operational efficiency and to avoid "unfairness" that might trigger mass surrenders of older policies
Distribution Channels: The intended method of sale dictates design; direct marketing requires simple products, whereas more complex "bells and whistles" may only be successful when explained by professional intermediaries

heading: 14.11 Regulatory constraints
text:
14.11 Regulatory constraints — Regulatory requirements:
Regulatory environments are significant drivers of product design, primarily aimed at protecting the interests of policyholders and ensuring the insurer remains solvent.

Restricts can apply to:  TRUST CARDS

heading: 14.2 Profitability
text:
14.2 Profitability — Profitability:
While the product is required to be profitable as whole, profitability is typically assessed across three dimensions:
- Savings: the company aims to make a profit on investment income by setting interest rate assumptions that are prudent relative to the expected investment environment.
- Charges must be sufficient to cover initial expenses, recurring expenses and portfolio set-up costs
- Profitability should be assessed against the company's required return or profit criteria
- Profitability will be sensitive to volumes, lapse rates, fund growth, expense overruns and the level of charges
- Protection: the pricing basis for mortality or morbidity must adequately cover the risks involved including expected future trends in experience.
- Administration: expense loadings must be set to cover marginal acquisition and administration costs, as well as providing a contribution toward the company's fixed overheads.

heading: 14.2 Profitability
text:
14.2 Profitability — Constraints on profitability:
Designers must also consider the impact on profitability of:
- Competition: insurers may lower the per-policy profit contribution to increase volumes or remain competitive in a market.
- Cross-subsidies: large policies may subsize the fixed costs of small policies to remain competitive across all sum assured bands.
- Regulatory requirements: regulatory caps on charges, legal requirement to treat customers fairly and meet policyholders reasonable expectations regarding profit distribution.

heading: 14.2 Profitability
text:
14.2 Profitability — Profit criteria:
NPV: discounted value of the profit signature using a risk discount rate, often expressed as a percentage of initial commission or the present value of future premiums
IRR: The discount rate at which the net present vales of cashflows equals zero
DPP: the time required for the accumulated profits discounted at the risk discount rate) to equal the initial investment

heading: 14.3 Marketability
text:
14.3 Marketability — Marketability:
Speaks the attractiveness of the product in the market:
- Customer needs: a product must be designed to meet specific financial needs.
- Affordability: premiums must be perceived as reasonable relative to benefits provided.
- Expectations: design choices must respect traditional practices e.g. level premiums
- Utility: maximizing the Utility of a product to the consumer.
- Distribution channels: the distribution channel will have a major influence on product design
- Volume of new business: Higher volumes could reduce per-policy fixed expense loadings

Insurers face market risk if they fail to manage policyholders expectations in the design phase due to reputation risk which could lead to loss of future sales.

heading: 14.4 Competitiveness
text:
14.4 Competitiveness — Factors influencing competitiveness:
- Distribution channels: The degree of price sensitivity depends heavily on the intended method of sale:
- Contract type: Different products compete on different elements of their pricing basis
- Term assurance:  mortality and fixed expense loadings
- Single premium endowments: interest rate assumption and expense loadings
- Savings products: past investment performance, charges and brand reputation
- Group life/pensions: customer service and administration

To avoid the race on price only, the company may seek product differentiation through
- Innovation: unique design features, options and guarantees
- Complexity: e.g. tiered benefits, bundled products

heading: 14.4 Competitiveness
text:
14.4 Competitiveness — The profit-volume relationship:
The primary objective is to maximize total contributions to the firms fixed overheads and profit from the product as a whole not per single policy.  $$[total \ contribution] = [per \ policy \ contribution] \times [number \ of \ policies \ sold]$$

Where the per-policy contribution is the profit from a single policy net of marginal costs (ignoring overhead costs).

The company's total profit is then:
$$[Total \ profit] = \left\{ \sum\limits_{all \ products} [total \ contributions] \right\} - [overheads] $$

In highly competitive markets, an insurer may choose a design with lower per-policy contributions to ensure high sales volume, thereby maximizing the total contribution.

heading: 14.4 Competitiveness
text:
14.4 Competitiveness — Constraints on competitiveness:
- Cross-Subsidies: A simple, competitive premium structure may require large policies to subsidize the fixed administrative costs of small policies to ensure the smaller policies do not appear unreasonably expensive to the public.

- Regulation: insurers are in competition with non-insurance companies (banks, unit-trusts and investment trust) for savings business, which are subject to different regulatory controls which may create a non-level playing field.

heading: 14.5 Financing requirements
callout_header: Reducing capital strain through policy features
text:
14.5 Financing requirements — Reducing capital strain through policy features:
- Actuarial Funding
- Negative non-unit reserves
- Clawback: using commission systems with a clawback clause, can reduce the company's exposure to non-recovery of initial expenses.
- Reserving basis: by increasing the valuation interest rate used for reserves, though this is subject to strict regulatory constraints and the availability of high-earning assets.

heading: 14.5 Financing requirements
text:
14.5 Financing requirements — Capital management:
The capital management strategy and availability of free assets will heavility influence product design:
- Recouping capital: the company's objective in capital management will heavily influence product design.
- Capital constraints: if a company has limited free assets, it must prioritize designs that minimize the initial capital requirement to ensure it remains solvent while meeting its sales goals.
- Opportunity cost: choosing to write capital-intensive business represents an opportunity costs, as that capital is no longer available to fund other investment/growth ventures.

heading: 14.5 Financing requirements
callout_header: How different product types and designs influence financing requirements
text:
14.5 Financing requirements — How different product types and designs influence financing requirements:
- Unit-Linked vs. Non-Linked: unit-linked products have significantly less capital requirements than non-linked products because they pass the investment risk to the policyholder and often have reviewable charges for mortality and expenses, leading to lower supervisory reserves.
- Guarantees: the inclusion of onerous guarantees (such as minimum maturity benefits or guaranteed annuity rates) increases the capital requirement because the insurer must hold additional reserves to cover the possibility of those guarantees "biting".
- Charging structures: charging structures that allow the company to recoup its initial expenses early are more capital efficient.
- Premium frequency: single premium contracts are more capital efficient than regular monthly premiums.

heading: 14.6 Risk characteristics
text:
14.6 Risk characteristics — Accepting risk:
The acceptability of a products design and risk profile depends on the company's willingness and ability to absorb risk internally or its capacity to transfer that risk.

If a company faces a large parameter risk (such as uncertain mortality rates in a new market), it may adjust the product design in several ways:
- Offering reviewable terms instead of long term guarantees, which allows the insurer to adjust charges if experience deteriorates
- Offering a unit-linked version of the product, which passes on the investment risk to the policyholder
- Reinsure a large part of the risk to limit its exposure
- Risk margins: incorporate ample risk margins in the premium rates to protect against adverse experience.
- Rider benefits: offer the contract as an additional rider benefit rather than a standalone.

file: 8. Product design/14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit.md
heading: 14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit
text:
14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit — Risks to the insurer:
Offering guarantees creates two significant risks for the insurer:

- Increased capital strain: supervisory regulations require companies to set up higher reserves to cover the possibility of a guarantee being exercised. This ties up more capital, increasing new business strain.
- Unexpected costs: While supervisory regulations require prudent assumptions to ensure a high probability that liabilities will be met, if actual market conditions deviate from the assumed conditions the cost of the guarantee biting may be in excess of the reserve.

file: 8. Product design/14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit.md
heading: 14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit
callout_header: Factors affecting the onerousness of guarantees
text:
14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit — Factors affecting the onerousness of guarantees:
The onerousness of any guarantee is determined by factors that influence both the potential for unexpected costs and the amount of capital the insurer must set aside from the outset.
- Size of the guarantee
- Duration
- Significance of reserves: the impact depends on the nature of the product, for instance a minimum investment yield guarantee is a much greater risk on a savings-heavy product than on a low reserve product like term assurance.
- Volume of business sold with the guarantee
- Available capital to absorb the initial reserving cost and potential pay outs
- The likelihood and impact of adverse changes
- Management actions

file: 8. Product design/14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit.md
heading: 14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit
text:
14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit — Sensitivity of profit:
Products are more likely to be sensitive to particular types of risks the more onerous the guarantees are. The components that affect profitability are:
- investment return
- mortality, or other contingency if relevant
- expenses, including expense inflation
- withdrawal rates

file: 8. Product design/14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit.md
heading: 14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit
callout_header: Product designs that reduce the sensitivity of profit to adverse experience
text:
14.7 Guarantees and sensitivity of profit — Product designs that reduce the sensitivity of profit to adverse experience:
The product design of a unit-linked contract can minimise the sensitivity of profitability by:
- Investment return: if there are no investment guarantees, then most of the risk is borne by the policyholder
- Mortality: reviewable charges at the company's discretion
- Withdrawal rates: don't offer any guaranteed surrender values
- Matching: try to match income (the charges) with outgo (expenses and benefit costs) as closely as possible by duration, especially with regard to initial expenses.

It may be possible to redesign non-linked contracts to reduce the sensitivity of profit to adverse variations in future experience  (e.g. by not offering any guaranteed surrender values, using commission systems with clawback for early withdrawals).

Non-linked with-profits contracts could be redesigned to reduce the guarantees associated with the bonus distribution method.

heading: 14.8 Cross subsidies
text:
14.8 Cross subsidies — Cross-subsidy definition:
Cross-subsidy refers to the sharing of non-risk elements, primarily expenses, where certain groups of policyholders contribute more than their fair share to support others. It is distinct from mutuality, which focuses on the pooling and sharing of insurance risks like mortality or investment volatility.

heading: 14.8 Cross subsidies
text:
14.8 Cross subsidies — Mutuality vs. Cross-Subsidy:
Mutuality involves the pooling and sharing of insurance risks (e.g., mortality, investment volatility) across policyholders. Cross-subsidy involves the sharing of non-risk elements — primarily expenses — where some policyholders pay more than their fair share to subsidize others. Cross-subsidy is a product design choice, while mutuality is a fundamental insurance principle.

heading: 14.8 Cross subsidies
text:
14.8 Cross subsidies — Cross-subsidy by policy/premium size:
Insurers incur fixed per-policy costs that remain constant regardless of the size of the policy.
Conflict: charging the full cost to small policies may make them uncompetitive or appear expensive to consumers.
Design solution: To ensure marketability, an actuary may design a product with a reduced fixed policy fee, recouping the shortfall by increasing the charges expressed as a percentage of the premium.
The result: this creates a cross-subsidy where larger policies overpay to subsidize the administration of smaller policies.
This may be viewed as unfair by policyholders that have large policies/premiums.

heading: 14.8 Cross subsidies
text:
14.8 Cross subsidies — Trade-off between simplicity and equity:
A major factor in product design is to manage the trade off between a simple, marketable charging structure and the desire to avoid cross-subsidies.
Simple structures often create unintentional cross-subsidies across different ages, terms, or policy sizes.
Any deliberate design that chooses not to reflect known differences in risk in the premium for marketing or simplicity reasons is seen as a cross-subsidy.

heading: 14.9 Administration systems
text:
14.9 Administration systems — Administration systems:
Administration systems are a primary practical constraint because the system requirements of a new product may limit the benefits provided or the charging structure adopted.

file: 9. Assumptions/Pricing assumptions/15.1 Assumptions as a source of risk.md
heading: 15.1 Assumptions as a source of risk
text:
15.1 Assumptions as a source of risk — Setting assumptions:
An insurer will make assumptions about future events to assess the eventual costs of its liabilities. Risk arises because these assumptions are made about an uncertain future, and reality will almost inevitably turn out differently from what was expected. Assumptions, cannot necessarily be matched by assets which protect the insurer from reality turning out differently from that assumed.

When the actual experience deviates from the assumptions, the decisions a company made regarding pricing, investment or reserving may no longer be appropriate, leading to financial losses or threats to solvency.
